note: This survey maps how educational data mining and learning analytics have grown since 2013, cataloguing methods, tools, datasets and trends, so AI in education researchers can see the field's current state and where it is heading.
title: Educational data mining and learning analytics: An updated survey

reading.body:
Educational data mining and learning analytics have grown into a broad, maturing field since 2013, with a shared toolkit of methods, tools and free datasets.

The survey's own framing is the useful part. It catalogues a knowledge discovery cycle, educational environments, specific tools, freely available datasets, common methods and main objectives, and it notes the proliferation of related names: Academic Analytics, Institutional Analytics, Teaching Analytics, Educational Data Science. A field that needs this many labels for overlapping work is one that has expanded faster than its vocabulary has settled.

For AI in education specifically, the practical consequence is that the inputs already exist. The survey points to free datasets and established methods, which means the constraint on this kind of work is not data collection or tooling. It is the same constraint that runs through everything else: the compute and the institutional systems needed to run analysis at scale, and the buildings and power behind them. The data here does not measure any of that, so the link is inference, not finding.

What the data does not cover is equally important. It is a survey, not a measurement, so it reports no growth rates, no adoption figures, no spending and no model performance. The citation count of 1068 shows the survey is widely referenced, which speaks to its standing as a map rather than to any result it establishes. A reader should treat it as a description of a field's shape, not as evidence about what that field has achieved.

explain_beginner: This paper looks at how researchers study data from education, such as information about students and how they learn. The authors updated an earlier survey from 2013 to show how much the field has grown. They describe the different names people now use for this work, the tools available, the free datasets, and the methods researchers apply. They also point to where the field is heading. It matters because it gives a clear picture of how data and AI are being used to understand and improve education, and it helps newcomers see the whole landscape in one place.
explain_business: This survey shows that using data and AI in education has grown a lot since 2013 and now covers many areas, from academic and institutional analytics to teaching analytics and data driven decision making. It catalogues the tools, datasets, methods, and trends that define the field today. For an executive, this means the space is broad and maturing, so any investment or strategy in education technology should account for these many subfields and the free resources already available. The decision it informs is how to scope and prioritise AI in education initiatives using a clear map of the current landscape.
explain_practitioner: This survey updates a 2013 review on data mining in education. The authors give a general overview of how Educational Data Mining and Learning Analytics are applied to educational data. They cover the main publications and milestones, the knowledge discovery cycle, educational environments, specific tools, freely available datasets, commonly used methods, main objectives, and future trends. They also note the many related terms now in use, such as Academic Analytics, Institutional Analytics, Teaching Analytics, and Educational Data Science. The key result is a current state of the art that maps the field's growth and direction since 2013.
